text: Hey all! I built Enzyme to help agents and people compound knowledge, together. This week I decided to open-source several years of my work (it began as an Obsidian plugin, then became the first MCP for Obsidian). Enzyme is like an LSP for ideas; it orients agents by emulating your working memory from a local knowledge base (sqlite or .md). I decided that a language was the best way to represent several design elements of agent memory at once: append-only log locations, temporal distribution config, profiles for "dreaming", and more. Your agent can setup Enzyme, compile the Enzyme program, and maintain a local-first, self-updating lens over its wiki. It's very fast. I use it daily to maintain my 8000+ note Zettelkasten that also acts as a personal CRM (meeting transcriptions), Readwise collection, journal, and home for agent rollout summaries. Core to its design are questions that are generated from recent material and projected over the corpus. Instead of "dreaming" .md files over fragments, it generates questions to connect their ideas using embedding similarity (static embeddings developed by Flower Computer). What these questions notice is configurable. The binary, including the embedding weights baked in, sits under 30 mb.
label: technical_explanation

text: > Why don't politicians care about this? Because it is not the subject that will win them the next election. And even if they care, some things are easier said than done. With politicians who care, you get things like GDPR, which goes in the right direction, but is a huge legal mess. And it is a mess because it can't be made simple. Obviously, you have to take consumer interests into account, but you also have to take companies interest into account too, both big and small, otherwise they will just stop doing business, which is bad for the economy and will mean that consumers won't find what they want at a reasonable price. You have to think about the loopholes big companies will invariably find, and covering them will add complexity, but still make it so that small companies can comply without a full time team of lawyers assisting them. For example, you say the consumer could return it for a full refund on a bad update, but to whom? Should the burden be put on the small retailer who sold it to you (and may be out of business)? There is already plenty of stuff the manufacturer must tell you, usually one a piece of paper no one reads, and the more you ask, the less people will read because there will be too much information. A "privacy score" may be a good idea, if well designed, it will share a place with the energy score, environment score, repairability score, safety signs, origin, etc... And how do you differentiate actual automated content recognition that consumers could want from spyware, formally, so that the first one is allowed but not the latter. All that to say that it is not impossible, but even with politicians caring, it is complicated. European politicians care (because it can win them votes), the results are so complicated they are getting ridiculed by the rest of the world.

text: It's not just index pages. Generally databases write records into pages, which are then grouped into extents. If the primary key gives an ordering you can create new pages and start filling them up in an orderly fashion. If it's random, you are doing random inserts into pages everywhere all the time, then you start running out of room in pages and have to start splitting them. UUIDv7 solves the most painful parts of this problem in general and is a much better option for a Primary Key than UUIDv1-4.

text: I've used FreeDNS on occasion for test domain names, one-off experiments, and similar. I'm very appreciative this exists, but there are some pain points that similar services handle better. The domains are missing from the public suffix list. This impacts how cookies are handled by the domain names, with concerns the browser will allow software to set the cookie on the shared domain name instead of the subdomain. This can be a security problem. Getting added to the PSL may not happen: https://github.com/publicsuffix/list/pull/79 It can be difficult to get a free HTTPS certificate for your subdomain. Let's Encrypt applies per-domain name rate limits and these domain names see lots of issuance requests. There's a process to lift those limits, but last I checked FreeDNS didn't use it. You can still, of course, pay for a certificate. There's tons of abuse on free domains so you may find that your domain is blocked on various lists. Here are some compelling alternatives I use now, which manage these issues better: - https://messwithdns.net/ - Exceptionally well-made DNS console for learning DNS - https://open-domains.com/ - Uses Cloudflare, great Discord group - Even more: https://free.hrsn.dev/#/?id=domains

text: GrapheneOS and AOSP are Linux distributions. Linux is not glibc, systemd, GNU coreutils, GCC and GNOME. Linux doesn't have a specific libc, init system, command-line utilities, compiler toolchain, graphical environment or other userspace components. There are many Linux distributions beyond Android not using those components. There's no standard Linux userspace and a distribution using OpenRC, musl, Clang/LLVM, uutils coreutils and other software isn't somehow not Linux. Linux distribution doesn't mean systemd/GNU/Linux. GrapheneOS and AOSP do use the userspace components developed with the Linux kernel such as iproute2. GNU components aren't part of Linux or the broader Linux project. Those don't even use a compatible license. It isn't legal to use the Linux kernel source code as a reference for writing glibc code since GPLv2-only does not permit the additional restrictions of GPLv3.
label: technical_explanation
